title: The Universal Role of Fragility on the Yielding Transition of Active Glass under Oscillatory Shear
authors: Arnab Mandal, Roni Chatterjee, Smarajit Karmakar
abstract: The yielding transition marks the onset of irreversible plastic deformation in amorphous solids and plays a central role in determining the mechanical stability and failure of metallic glasses, colloidal suspensions, and biological assemblies. Despite extensive research, the microscopic factors governing the nature of yielding, particularly the transition between brittle and ductile mechanical responses, remain poorly understood. Recent studies have identified kinetic fragility as a key parameter governing yielding in passive glasses; whether this connection persists in active glasses remains open. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations of a Kob-Andersen glass former doped with Run-and-Tumble (RTP) active particles under oscillatory shear, we show that activity systematically reduces kinetic fragility and consequently alters the mechanical response. The common yield point $γ_c$ decreases monotonically with activity and exhibits a power-law dependence on the Arrhenius activation barrier. Increasing activity suppresses the dependence of the yield strain on thermal history and transforms the response from brittle-like to increasingly ductile, with smoother stress relaxation and reduced stress discontinuities. The timescale to reach steady state near yielding retains a critical power-law divergence, indicating that activity does not alter the underlying critical character of the transition. Active glasses also develop broader, more diffuse shear bands. Our results establish kinetic fragility as a unifying parameter governing yielding in both passive and active glasses and demonstrate that activity offers a powerful route to tune the mechanical response of amorphous materials.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations to study active glasses, showing that self-propulsion systematically reduces the material's kinetic fragility. This activity-induced change fundamentally alters the mechanical response, making the material more ductile and establishing fragility as a universal descriptor for yielding in both passive and active amorphous solids.
main_problem: The study investigates how the introduction of activity (self-propulsion) modifies the fundamental physical parameter, kinetic fragility, that governs the yielding transition in amorphous solids.
main_result: Activity systematically reduces kinetic fragility, shifts the mechanical response from brittle to ductile, and establishes kinetic fragility as a unifying parameter for yielding in both passive and active glasses.
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are used to model the system's response to oscillatory shear, analyzing structural relaxation and mechanical failure.
model_or_system: The model uses a Kob-Andersen glass former doped with Run-and-Tumble (RTP) active particles, simulating the system's dynamics under oscillatory shear stress.
key_observables: Kinetic fragility ($K_{	ext{VFT}}$), common yield point ($\gamma_c$), yield strain ($\gamma_y$), stress relaxation profiles, and shear band morphology.
important_parameters: Activity parameters ($ho_a, f_0, 	au_p$), temperature ($T$), and shear strain amplitude ($\gamma_{max}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on extending the concept of kinetic fragility, previously established for passive glasses, to the active regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of structural relaxation time ($	au_\alpha$) with activity, the shift from brittle to ductile yielding behavior, and the dependence of the yield point on thermal history.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the role of fragility in passive glasses, then introduces active particles via MD simulations, and finally quantifies how activity systematically modifies the yield point, mechanical response, and underlying critical dynamics.
why_interesting: While focused on classical soft matter, the concept of tuning material response (brittle to ductile) via an active driving force is relevant to non-equilibrium dynamics and energy dissipation in complex quantum or mesoscopic systems.
